title: Optimal Biomass Allocation to Leaves Across Global Terrestrial Ecosystems
content:
This study presents an optimality-based theory that integrates leaf economic traits and the leaf area index–biomass production ratio to predict leaf carbon allocation from environmental conditions. The theory explains global patterns of leaf carbon allocation and predicts a progressive decline in biomass allocated to leaves under rising atmospheric CO2.


ABSTRACT

Leaves influence global climate and water resources by regulating the flows of CO2, energy and water between the atmosphere and land. Here we developed a theoretical framework that predicts the optimal annual fraction of biomass production allocated to the production of new leaves (η f) as the product of the optimal leaf area index (LAI) and the optimal ratio of leaf mass–per–area to the leaf life cycle (LMA/LC), divided by annual total biomass production (BP). All quantities depend on local environmental variables, with different solutions (embedding a climatic aridity effect on optimal LMA/LC) for evergreen and deciduous plants. Using a global compilation of η f data, we show that this theory predicts the emergent responses of η f to growing–season temperature and aridity. These responses arise from the trade-offs among the environmental sensitivities of LMA/LC, LAI and BP. It is predicted that the rising CO2 is steadily reducing the fraction of biomass production allocated to leaves.
